title: Erdoğan's UNGA Push to Abolish UNSC Veto Draws Kremlin Rejection as Turkey Sets Out Maximalist Agenda
subhead: At the 81st UN General Assembly, President Erdoğan called for stripping permanent Security Council members of their veto power, reiterated recognition of Palestinian statehood, and pressed Turkish Cypriot sovereignty — while the Kremlin quickly rejected the veto plan and Trump courted Erdoğan at a Gulf summit in New York.

sections.heading: Erdoğan's UNSC Veto Abolition Call and Russia's Rejection
sections.body:
In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, President Erdoğan proposed abolishing the veto power of the UN Security Council's five permanent members, arguing the body has been 'rendered unable to fulfil its mission.' TRT World, Arab News and Ukrinform all reported the proposal, which Ankara framed as part of a broader demand for UN reform.

The push drew a swift rebuke from Moscow: Türkiye Today reported that the Kremlin rejected Erdoğan's call to scrap the veto, underscoring the limits of even the close Erdogan-Putin channel on institutional questions. Ankara also used the platform to urge wider recognition of a Palestinian state, per Reuters, and raised Kashmir, calling for it to 'be addressed through dialogue,' according to the Hindustan Times.
sections.whyItMatters: The veto proposal is a familiar Ankara talking point, but pairing it with UNGA — while Russia and the US are both active in New York — tests whether Turkey can position itself as a champion of the Global South without fracturing its ties to either veto-holding power.

sections.heading: Trump Courts Erdoğan at GCC Summit
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump described Erdoğan as a friend, 'a tough cookie' and 'a great guy' during a Gulf Cooperation Council meeting on the sidelines of UNGA that Erdoğan also attended, alongside Jordan's King Abdullah, Qatar's Emir and Syria's Ahmed al-Sharaa, Türkiye Today reported. Trump used the session to detail his Iran campaign, claiming roughly 99 percent of US military action was aimed at preventing an Iranian nuclear bomb, and to tout the reopened Strait of Hormuz, saying more oil now transits the waterway than at any point since the conflict began.

The meeting came as Washington works on a postwar regional strategy expected to be finalized after November's US midterms, per the report. Trump also referenced a Gaza cease-fire deal that he said had saved many lives.
sections.whyItMatters: The warm tone deepens the US-Turkey thaw under Erdoğan's presidency, but Ankara's maximalist UN messaging and its independent line on Iran and Gaza mean the chemistry is personal more than structural — policy gaps remain.

sections.heading: Erdoğan and Guterres: Gaza, Black Sea and Iran
sections.body:
Following his address, Erdoğan met UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in New York, telling him that Israel's 'lack of willingness' to pursue peace in Gaza had 'once again become apparent,' and that settler attacks in the West Bank and assaults on Jerusalem's holy sites had worsened the situation, Türkiye Today reported, citing the presidency's Communications Directorate.

Erdoğan stressed the need to preserve the basis for a two-state solution. He also said Turkey was working to support diplomatic processes on Iran and Ukraine, floated a regionally-driven outcome on the Strait of Hormuz, and raised concerns over commercial vessels being targeted in the Black Sea, calling for responsible behavior by all parties to safeguard navigation.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is positioning itself as a mediator across multiple theatres — Gaza, Ukraine, Iran and the Black Sea — even as the US-Iran conflict and Gaza cease-fire dynamics dominate the summit agenda.

sections.heading: Cyprus: Ankara Demands Sovereign Equality and an East Med Conference
sections.body:
Erdoğan used UNGA to reiterate Ankara's hard line on Cyprus, telling Guterres that no proposal would produce results unless it recognized 'the sovereign equality and equal international status' of Turkish Cypriots, and calling for an East Mediterranean conference, per The National Herald, tovima and kiprinform. The two leaders also exchanged views on Cyprus, Ukraine and the wider Middle East, the UN said.

The position restates the two-state framework Ankara has pursued since 2021, after the collapse of the UN-mediated talks in Crans-Montana, and comes as Cyprus remains split between the internationally recognized Republic and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognized only by Turkey.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is using the UNGA moment to push its sovereign-equality doctrine at the highest level, likely complicating any renewed UN effort on Cyprus and setting up friction with Athens and Nicosia.

sections.heading: Fidan UN Secretary-General Speculation and the 'Gender Neutrality' Message
sections.body:
Israeli media, via The Jerusalem Post, reported that Israel is closely watching whether Erdoğan will push Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan as a candidate for UN secretary-general as Guterres' tenure nears its end. Fidan met Guterres in New York alongside Erdoğan and discussed Cyprus, Syria and regional issues, per Anadolu Agency and TRT World.

Separately, Ynetnews reported that Erdoğan targeted 'gender neutrality' at the UN after sweeping LGBTQ+ raids across Turkey, framing gender-neutral policies as targeting children and the family. The UNGA platform gave Ankara a global stage for its social-conservative agenda amid intensified domestic enforcement.
sections.whyItMatters: The Fidan story signals a potential post-2026 transition play for Turkey's top diplomat, while the gender-neutrality remarks tie domestic cultural policy to Ankara's UN diplomacy — an unusual pairing that may sharpen Western criticism.

sections.heading: Uganda Suspends Military Cooperation With Ankara
sections.body:
Uganda's military (UPDF) abruptly suspended all military and defense cooperation with Türkiye, escalating a diplomatic row that began with Ankara's refusal to extradite dissident blogger Fred Lumbuye, who has lived in Turkey since 2013, Türkiye Today reported. The suspension followed demonstrations by supporters of Uganda's Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba outside Turkey's embassy in Kampala.

Türkiye Today's analysis argues the real driver is economic: Uganda's Somalia mission is ending, cutting off $60-72 million a year in per-soldier payments, while Turkey has become Somalia's dominant security partner — running TURKSOM, training over 25,000 Somali soldiers, and hosting F-16s, Akinci and TB2 drones under a 2024 framework defense agreement.
sections.whyItMatters: The rupture exposes a sharper version of intra-Islamic/African competition: as Ankara consolidates its position in Somalia and the Horn, older troop-contributing states like Uganda are feeling the financial squeeze and pushing back.

bottomLine: Erdoğan's UNGA week is a bid to claim the Global South mantle — abolishing the UNSC veto, recognizing Palestine and Turkish Cypriot sovereignty, and positioning Fidan for the UN's top job — while simultaneously locking in warm personal ties with Trump in New York. Moscow's quick rejection of the veto plan shows the ceiling on that activism, and Uganda's suspension of military cooperation shows the cost of Ankara's expanding footprint in Africa and the Horn. The immediate question for Washington is whether the personal chemistry with Erdoğan translates into concrete bargains on F-16s and regional security before the US midterms refocus American attention.
sources: TRT World, Arab News, Ukrinform, Reuters, Türkiye Today, UN News, The Jerusalem Post, Hindustan Times, Ynetnews, The National Herald, tovima, kiprinform, Anadolu Agency, AFP
